idiom_name: private lock object with synchronized blocks; Mutex.withLock when suspending
implementation_notes: Kotlin on the JVM inherits the monitor model, so the guardian is a private lock instance of its own (`private val lock = Any()`, or a `ReentrantLock`) around private state, with `synchronized(lock) { ... }` delimiters - not `@Synchronized` on a public method, which locks `this` and lets callers take the same monitor. The JVM supplies the visibility guarantee (monitor enter/exit happens-before), and the lock must be a distinct object that never escapes the class. For suspending code the blocking form is the wrong guardian: `kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex` with `withLock` is the same pattern in suspending form, documented as non-reentrant with memory semantics similar to `synchronized`, and it suspends the coroutine instead of blocking a thread - the documented choice when the protected state cannot be confined to a single thread.
pitfalls: `@Synchronized` (and plain `synchronized {}`) locks the receiver: on a public object that is the same as publishing the lock, so accidental deadlock with caller code becomes possible.

An `unlock()` without its matching `lock()` - or an exception between them - throws on the JVM and leaves the guardian broken; use `withLock { }`, which is documented as `lock(); try { ... } finally { unlock() }`.
A `Mutex` is non-reentrant: a `withLock` nested inside another `withLock` on the same mutex deadlocks, which is usually the sign that the guarded operations are too fragmented.

variants.name: kotlinx.coroutines Mutex with withLock
variants.implementation_notes: When the guarded work must suspend, a `kotlinx.coroutines.sync.Mutex` is the guardian: `withLock` delimits the critical section, `lock()` suspends the coroutine instead of blocking a thread, and the mutex is explicitly non-reentrant, so a nested acquisition deadlocks rather than silently recursing. The docs describe the JVM memory semantics as similar to a `synchronized` block, and `unlock` throwing when the caller is not the owner makes misuse loud. Keep it for state that genuinely must be shared between coroutines on different threads; otherwise the documented finer alternatives - a single-threaded context (thread confinement) or an atomic/thread-safe holder - are cheaper than serialising.
pitfalls: Blocking calls (`Thread.sleep`, IO without a dispatcher, `runBlocking`) inside `withLock` suspend nothing and hold the mutex across a blocked thread.
A `Mutex` held across a suspension point that itself acquires the same mutex (directly or through a helper) deadlocks, because the lock is not reentrant.
